RTF format
 
and a

.

Note that in the following translation the numbers 
without brackets refer to this text, while the numbers in square brackets refer 
to the Greek text. In the English text line numbers short indented lines are 
usually included with the short preceding line (as a single line) in the 
reckoning. Links to explanatory endnotes are indicated by an underlined 
number in brackets: e.g.,  
 
(23)
. 
These have been provided by the translator. Stage directions have also been 
added by the translator.

 

In this translation, 
possessives of words ending in -s are usually indicated in the common way (that 
is, by adding 
-âs
 (e.g. 
Zeus
 and 
Zeusâs
). This 
convention adds a syllable to the spoken word (the sound 
-iz
). 
Sometimes, for metrical reasons, this English text indicates such possession in 
an alternate manner, with a simple apostrophe. This form of the possessive does 
not add an extra syllable to the spoken name (e.g., 
Orestes 
and 

Orestesâ
 are both three-syllable words; whereas, 
Orestesâ
s has 
four syllables).
 

 

The translator would like to acknowledge the 
valuable help he received from the notes in Alan H. Sommersteinâs edition of 

Birds 
(Warminster: Aris and Phillips, 1987).

 

HISTORICAL NOTE

 

Birds 
 
was first produced at the drama festival 
in 414 BC, where it won second prize. At this period, during the Peloponnesian 
War, Athens was very powerful and confident, having just launched the expedition 
to Sicily, fully expecting to triumph in that venture and in the larger war.

 

 

DRAMATIS PERSONAE

 

PISTHETAIROS: a middle-aged 
Athenian

EUELPIDES: a middle-aged Athenian

SERVANT-BIRD: a slave serving Tereus, once a man

TEREUS: a hoopoe bird, once a man

FLAMINGO

PEACOCK

A SECOND HOOPOE

GLUTTON-BIRD: a fictitious species

CHORUS LEADER

CHORUS: of birds

XANTHIAS: slave serving Pisthetairos

MANODOROS: slave serving Euelpides, also called MANES.

PROCNE: a nightingale with a womanâs body, consort of 
Tereus.

PRIEST

POET

ORACLE MONGER: a collector and interpreter of oracles

METON: a land surveyor

COMMISSIONER OF COLONIES: an Athenian official

STATUTE SELLER: man who sells laws

FIRST MESSENGER: a construction-worker bird

SECOND MESSENGER: a soldier bird

IRIS: messenger goddess, daughter of Zeus

FIRST HERALD: a bird

YOUNG MAN: young Athenian who wants to beat up his 
father

CINESIAS: a very bad dithyrambic poet and singer

SYCOPHANT: a common informer

PROMETHEUS: a Titan

POSEIDON: god of the sea, brother of Zeus

HERCULES: the legendary hero, now divine

TRIBALLIAN GOD: an uncouth barbarian god

PRINCESS: a divine young lady

SECOND HERALD

 

[A rugged, treed wilderness area up in the rocky hills. 
Enter Pisthetairos and Euelpides, both very tired. They are clambering down from 
the rocky heights towards the level stage. Pisthetairos has a crow perched on 
his arm or shoulder, and Euelpides has a jackdaw. Both Pisthetairos and 
Euelpides are carrying packs on their back. They are followed by two slaves 
carrying more bags. The slaves stay well out of the way until they get involved 
in the action later on.]

 

EUELPIDES 
[speaking to the bird he is carrying]

Are you telling us to keep 
going straight ahead?

Over there by that tree?

 

PISTHETAIROS

                                                   Blast this birdâ

itâs croaking for us to head back, go home.

 

EUELPIDES    

Why are we wandering up and 
down like this?

Youâre such a foolâthis endless weaving round

will kill us both.

 

PISTHETAIROS

                                         I must be an idiot

to keep hiking on along these pathways,

a hundred miles at least, and just because

thatâs what this crow keeps telling me to do.

 

EUELPIDES

What about me? My poor toe 
nails are thrashed.                        

  10

Iâve worn them out because Iâm following

what this jackdaw says.

 

PISTHETAIROS 
[looking around]

                                      I have no idea

where on earth we are.

 

EUELPIDES

                                      You mean from here

you couldnât make it back to your place?                                           

   

   [10]

 

PISTHETAIROS

No wayânot even
 
Execestides

could manage that.
(1)

 

EUELPIDES

                      Weâre in a real mess.

 

PISTHETAIROS

Well, you could try going along that pathway.

 

[The two men start exploring different paths down to 
opposite sides of the stage.]

 

EUELPIDES

We two were conned by that 
Philokrates,

the crazy vendor in the marketplace

who sells his birds on trays. He claimed these two                      

  20

would take us straight to Tereus the hoopoe,

a man who years ago became a bird.

Thatâs why we paid an obol for 
 
this 
one,

this jackdaw,  a son of Tharreleides,

and three more for the crow.
(2)
 And then what?

The two know nothing, except how to bite.

 

[The jackdaw with Euelpides begins to get excited 
about something. Euelpides talks to the bird.]

 

Whatâs got your attention now? 
In those rocks                                    

    [20]

You want to take us there? Thereâs no way through.

                   
 

PISTHETAIROS 
[calling across the stage to Euelpides]

By god, the same thing over here, no road.

 

EUELPIDES

Whatâs your crow saying about the pathway?                             

  30

 

PISTHETAIROS

By god, itâs not cawing what it did before.

 

EUELPIDES 
[shouting]

But whatâs it saying about the road?

 

PISTHETAIROS

                                                             Nothingâ

itâs saying nothing, just keeps on croakingâ

something about biting my fingers off.

 

EUELPIDES 
[addressing the audience]

Donât you think itâs really odd 
the two of us,

ready and eager to 
 
head off to the 
birds,

just canât find the way.
(3)
 
You see, weâre not well.

All you men sitting there to hear our words,                                        

    [30]

weâre ill with a disease, not like the one

which Sacas suffers, noâthe opposite.
(4)
                                     

  40

Heâs no true citizen, yet nonetheless

heâs pushing his way in by force, but we,

both honoured members of our tribe and clan,

both citizens among you citizens,

with no one trying to drive us from the city,

have winged our
 way out of our native 
land

on our two feet.
(5)
 
We donât hate the city

because we think itâs not by nature great

and truly prosperousâopen to all,

so they can spend their money paying fines.                                

  50
     

Cicadas chirp up in the trees a while,

a month or two, but our Athenians                                                       

   [40]

keep chirping over lawsuits all their lives. 

Thatâs why right now weâve set off on this trip,

with all this stuffâbasket, pot, and myrtle boughs.
(6)

Weâre looking for a nice relaxing spot,

where we can settle down, live out our lives.

Weâre heading for Tereus, that hoopoe birdâ

weâd like to know if in his flying around

heâs seen a city like the one we want.                                           

   60

 

PISTHETAIROS

Hey!

 

EUELPIDES

            What?

 

PISTHETAIROS

                       My crow keeps cawing upwardsâup there.

 

EUELPIDES

My jackdaw is looking up there, too,                                                     

   [50]

as if it wants to show me something.

There must be birds around these rocks. I knowâ

letâs make noise and then weâll see for sure.

 

PISTHETAIROS

You know what you should do? Kick that outcrop.

 

EUELPIDES

Why not use your head? Thereâd be twice the noise.

 

[
Pisthetairos and 
Euelpides start climbing back up the rocky outcrops towards a door in the middle 
of the rocks.]

 

PISTHETAIROS

Pick up a stone and then knock on the door.

 

EUELPIDES

All right. Here I go.

 

[
Euelpides knocks very loudly on 
the door and calls out.]

 

                               Hey, boy . . . boy!

 

PISTHETAIROS

What are you saying? Why call 
the hoopoe âboyâ?                      

   70

Donât say thatâyou should call out

[Giving a bird call]

   
                                                       
âHoopoe-ho!â

 

EUELPIDES 
[knocking on the 
door and calling again]

Hoopoe-ho! . . . Should I knock again? . . . Hoopoe-ho!

 

SERVANT-BIRD 
[inside]

Who is it? Whoâs shouting for my master?                                           

  [60]

 

[The door opens and an actor-bird emerges. He has a 
huge beak which terrifies Euelpides and Pisthetairos. They fall back in fear, 
and the birds they have been carrying disappear.]

 

EUELPIDES

My lord Apollo, save us! That gaping beakâ

 

SERVANT-BIRD 
[also 
frightened]

Oh, oh, now weâre in for it. 
You two men,

youâre bird-catchers!

 

EUELPIDES

                       Donât act so weird!

Canât you say something nice?

 

SERVANT-BIRD 
[trying to 
scare them off]

                                      

You two men will die!

 

EUELPIDES

But weâre not men.

 

SERVANT-BIRD

                       What? What are you, then?

 

EUELPIDES

Well . . . Iâm a chicken-shitter . . . a Libyan bird . . 
.

 

SERVANT-BIRD

Thatâs rubbish.

 

EUELPIDES

                   Itâs notâIâve just dropped my loadâ                        

  80

down both my legs. Take a look.

 

SERVANT-BIRD

                                          And this one here?

What kind of bird is he?

[To Pisthetairos]

 

                     
                             

Can you speak?

 

PISTHETAIROS

Me? . . . a crapper-fowl . . . from Phasis.

 

EUELPIDES

God knows what kind of animal you are!

 

SERVANT-BIRD

Iâm a servant bird.

 

EUELPIDES

                              Beaten by some rooster                                            

    [70]

in a cock fight?

 

SERVANT-BIRD

                                  No. It was my masterâ

when he became a hoopoe, well, I prayed

that I could turn into a bird. That way

heâd still have me to serve and wait on him.

 

EUELPIDES

Does a bird need his own butler bird?                                          

90

 

SERVANT-BIRD

He doesâI think itâs got 
something to do

with the fact that earlier he was a man.

So if he wants to taste some fish from Phalerum,

I grab a plate and run off for sardines.

If he wants soup, we need pot and ladle,

so I dash off for the spoon.

 

EUELPIDES

                                                  A runner birdâ

thatâs what you are. Well, my little runner,

do you know what weâd like to have you do?                                    

    

   [80]

Go call your master for us.

 

SERVANT-BIRD

                                          But heâs asleepâ

for heavenâs sake, his after-dinner snoozeâ                         

        

 100

heâs just had gnats and myrtle berries.

 

EUELPIDES

Wake him up anyway.

 

SERVANT-BIRD

                                            I know for sure

heâll be annoyed, but Iâll do it, just for you.

 

[Exit Servant-Bird back through the doors.]

 

PISTHETAIROS

Damn that birdâhe scared me half to death.

 

EUELPIDES

Bloody hellâhe frightened off my bird!

 

PISTHETAIROS

Youâre such a cowardâthe worst 
there is.

Were you so scared you let that jackdaw go?

 

EUELPIDES

What about you? Didnât you 
collapse

and let your crow escape?  

 

PISTHETAIROS

                                          
Not me, by god!

 

EUELPIDES

Where is it then?

 

PISTHETAIROS 

                          It flew off on its own.                                            

110
     
   [90]

 

EUELPIDES

You didnât let go? What a valiant man!

 

TEREUS: 
[from inside, speaking in a grand style]

Throw open this wood, so I may issue forth.

 

[The doors open. Enter Tereus, a hoopoe bird, with 
feathers on his head and wings but none on his body. He struts and speaks with a 
ridiculously affected confidence. Euelpides and Pisthetairos are greatly amused 
at his appearance.]

 

EUELPIDES

O Hercules, what kind of beast 
is this?

Whatâs that plumage? What sort of triple crest?

 

TEREUS

Who are the persons here who 
seek me out?

 

EUELPIDES

The twelve gods, it seems, have worked you over.
(7)

 

TEREUS

Does seeing my feathers make 
you scoff at me?

Strangers, I was once upon a time a man.

 

EUELPIDES

Itâs not you weâre laughing at.

 

TEREUS

                                         Then what is it?

 

EUELPIDES

Itâs your beakâto us it looks 
quite funny.                                   

 120

 

TEREUS

Itâs how Sophocles distorts 
Tereusâ                                                    

    [100]

thatâs meâin his tragedies.

 

EUELPIDES

                             
Youâre Tereus?

Are you a peacock or a bird?
(8)

 

TEREUS

                                     I am a bird.

 

EUELPIDES

Then where are all your feathers?

 

TEREUS

                                              Theyâve fallen off.

 

EUELPIDES

Have you got some disease?

 

TEREUS          

                                                No, itâs not that.

In winter time all birds shed their feathers,

then new ones grow again. But tell me thisâ

who are the two of you?

 

EUELPIDES

                          Us? Weâre human beings.

 

TEREUS

From what race were you born?

 

EUELPIDES

                                                            Our origin?

In Athensâwhich makes the finest warships.                        

      

 130

 

TEREUS

Ah, so youâre jury-men, are you?

 

EUELPIDES

                                                             No, no.

Weâre differentâwe keep away from juries.

 

TEREUS

Does that seedling flourish in those parts?                                          

    [110]

 

EUELPIDES

If you go searching in the countryside,

youâll find a few.

 

TEREUS

                             So why have you come here?

What do you need?

 

EUELPIDES

                        To talk to you.

 

TEREUS

                                              What for? 

 

EUELPIDES

Well, you were once a man, as we are now.

You owed people money, as we do now.

You loved to skip the debt, as we do now.

Then you changed your nature, became a bird.                            

140

You fly in circles over land and sea.

Youâve learned whateverâs known to birds and men.

Thatâs why weâve come as suppliants to you,                                       

     [120]

to ask if you can tell us of some town,

where life is sheepskin soft, where we can sleep.

 

TEREUS

Are you looking for a mighty city,

more powerful than what Cranaus built?
(9)

 

EUELPIDES

Not one more powerful, no. What we want

is one which better suits the two of us.

 

TEREUS

You clearly want an aristocracy.                                                   

  150

 

EUELPIDES

Me? No, not at all. The 

son of Scellias

is someone I detest.
(10)

 

TEREUS

                                                   All right, then,

What kind of city would you like to live in?

 

EUELPIDES

Iâd like a city where my biggest problem

would be something like thisâin the morning

a friend comes to my door and says to me,

âIn the name of Olympian Zeus, take a bath,                                        

   [130]

an early one, you and your children,

then come to my place for the wedding feast

Iâm putting on. Donât disappoint me now.                                    

 160

If you do, then donât come looking for
 me

when my affairs get difficult for me.â
(11)

 

TEREUS

By heaven, you poor man, you do love trouble.

What about you?

 

PISTHETAIROS

                          Iâd like the same.

 

TEREUS

                                                           Like what?

 

PISTHETAIROS

To have the father of some handsome lad

come up to me, as if Iâd done him wrong,

and tell me off with some complaint like thisâ

âA fine thing there between you and my son,                                       

   [140]

you old spark. You met him coming back

from the gymnasium, after his bathâ                                           

170

you didnât kiss or greet him with a hug,

or even try tickling his testiclesâ

yet youâre a friend of mine, his father.â

 

TEREUS

How you yearn for problems, you unhappy man.

There is a happy city by the sea,

the Red Sea, just like the one you mention.
(12)

 

EUELPIDES

No, no. Not by the sea! Thatâs not for us,

not where that ship Salamia can show up

with some man on board to serve a summons

early in the morning. What about 
 
Greece?                            
 

       

  180

Can you tell us of some city there?
(13)

 

TEREUS

Why not go and settle down in Elisâ

in Lepreus?

 

EUELPIDES

                                      In Leprous? By the gods,

I hate the placeâalthough 
 
Iâve never seen itâ                                  

  

    [150]

itâs all Melanthiusâs fault.
(14)

 

TEREUS

                                          You could go

to the Opuntiansâtheyâre in Locrisâ

you might settle there.

 

EUELPIDES

                                                 Be Opuntiusâ

no way, not for a talentâs weight in gold.
(15)

But whatâs it like here, living with the birds?

You must know it well.

 

TEREUS

                                            Itâs not unpleasant.                             

 190

First of all, you have to live without a purse.

 

EUELPIDES

So youâre rid of one great source of fraud in life.

 

TEREUS

In the gardens we enjoy white sesame,                                                 

    [160]

the myrtles, mint, and poppies.           
 

 

EUELPIDES

                                  So you live

just like newly-weds.

 

PISTHETAIROS

                                   Thatâs it! Iâve got it!

I see a great plan for this race of birdsâ

and power, too, if youâll trust what I say.

 

TEREUS

What do you want to get us all to do?

 

PISTHETAIROS

What should you be convinced to do? Well, first,

donât just fly about in all directions,                                              

 200

your beaks wide openâthat makes you despised.

With us, you see, if you spoke of men

who always flit about and if you asked,

âWhoâs that Teleasâ someone would respond,

âThe manâs a birdâheâs unreliable,

flighty, vague, never stays in one place long.â
(16)
                                  

    [170]

 

TEREUS

By Dionysus, thatâs a valid pointâ

the criticismâs fair. What should we do?

 

PISTHETAIROS

Settle down together in one city.

 

TEREUS

What sort of city could we birds set up?                                     

   210

 

PISTHETAIROS

Why ask that? What a stupid thing to say!

Look down.

 

TEREUS

                           
All right.

 

PISTHETAIROS

                                 
      Now look up.

 

TEREUS

                                                           I'm looking up.

 

PISTHETAIROS

Turn your head round to the side.

 

TEREUS

                                                      
By Zeus,

thisâll do me good, if I twist off my neck.

 

PISTHETAIROS

What do you see?

 

TEREUS

                   
Clouds and sky.

 

PISTHETAIROS

                                        Well, then,

isnât this a staging area for birds?

 

TEREUS

A staging area? How come itâs that?

 

PISTHETAIROS

You might say itâs a location for themâ                                               

    [180]

thereâs lots of business here, but everything

keeps moving through this zone, so itâs now called                      

 220

a staging place. But if you settled here,

fortified it, and fenced it off with walls,

this staging area could become your state.

Then youâd rule all men as if theyâre locusts

and annihilate the 
 
gods with famine,

just like in Melos.
(17)

 

TEREUS

                           Howâd we manage that?

 

PISTHETAIROS

Look, between earth and heaven thereâs the air.

Now, with us, when we want to go to Delphi,

we have to ask permission to pass through

from the Boeotians. You should do the same.                               

 230

When men sacrifice, make gods pay you cash.                                     

    [190]

If not, you donât grant them rights of passage.

Youâll stop the smell of roasting thigh bones

moving through an empty space and city

which donât belong to them.

 

TEREUS

                                                                    Wow!!! Yippee!!

By earth, snares, traps, nets, what a marvellous 
scheme!

Iâve never heard a neater plan! So now,

with your help, Iâm going to found a city,

if other birds agree.

 

PISTHETAIROS

                                                    The other birds?

Whoâs going to lay this business out to them?                        

      

240

 

TEREUS

You can do it. Iâve taught them how to speak.                                      

   [200]

Before I came, they could only twitter,

but Iâve been with them here a long, long time.

 

PISTHETAIROS

How do you call to bring them all together?

 

TEREUS

Easy. Iâll step inside my thicket here,

and wake my nightingale. Then weâll both call.

Once they hear our voices theyâll come running.

 

PISTHETAIROS

O, you darling bird, now donât just stand thereâ

not when Iâm begging you to go right now,

get in your thicket, wake your nightingale
.                                    
 

250

 

[
Tereus goes back through the doors]
(18)

 

TEREUS 
[singing]

Come my queen, donât sleep so long,

pour forth the sound of sacred songâ                                                  

   [210]

lament once more through lips divine

for Itys, your dead child and mine,

the one weâve cried for all this time.
(19)

 

Sing out your musicâs liquid trill

in that vibrato voiceâthe thrill

which echoes in those purest tones

through leafy haunts of yew trees roams

and rises up to Zeusâs throne.                                                        

  260

Apollo with the golden hair

sits listening to your music thereâ

and in response he plucks his stringâ

his lyre of ivory then brings

the gods themselves to dance and sing.

Then from godsâ mouths in harmony                                                    

    [220]

come sounds of sacred melody.

 

[A flute starts playing within, in imitation of the 
nightingaleâs song. The melody continues for a few moments]

 

EUELPIDES

By lord Zeus, that little birdieâs got a voice!

She pours her honey all through that thicket!

 

PISTHETAIROS

Hey!

 

EUELPIDES

         What?

 

PISTHETAIROS

                  Shut up.

 

EUELPIDES

                             Why?

 

PISTHETAIROS

                                    That hoopoe birdâ                                    

 270
 

heâs all set to sing another song.

 

TEREUS 
[issuing a bird call to all the birds. His song 
or chant is accompanied by the flute indicating the nightingaleâs song]

Epo-popo-popo-popo-popoi,

Io, io, ito, ito, ito, ito.

Come here to me,

all you with feathers just like mine,                                                        

 [230]

all you who live in country fields

fresh-ploughed, still full of seed,

and all you thousand tribes

who munch on barley corn

who gather up the grain,                                                                

 280

and fly at such a speed

and utter your sweet cries,

all you who in the furrows there

twitter on the turned-up earth,

and sweetly sing

tio tio tio tio tio tio tio tio.

All those of you

who like to scavenge food

from garden ivy shoots,                                                                          

   [240]

all you in the hills up there                                                             

 290

who eat from olive and arbutus trees.

come here as quickly as you can,

fly here in answer to this callâ

trio-to trio-to toto-brix!

And every one of you

in low-lying marshy ground

who snap sharp-biting gnats,

by regions of well-watered land,

and lovely fields of Marathon,

all you variously coloured birds,                                                    

  300

godwits and francolinsâ

Iâm calling you.
